CHIEF COMPLAINT
Evaluation of kidney stones

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a male presenting for evaluation of kidney stones. Approximately one week ago, while working in a barn moving hay with horses, he developed sudden onset of right-sided back pain. He initially attributed this to the physical activity but quickly developed associated diaphoresis and nausea. He sought evaluation from his primary care physician who ordered a CT scan confirming the presence of a kidney stone. The pain radiated almost to the groin area. Since the initial episode, he has experienced intermittent pain of shorter duration. He has been straining his urine as instructed but has not observed any stone fragments. He denies hematuria and states his urine has not appeared darker than usual. This is his first kidney stone. Father has a history of recurrent kidney stones.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Denies fever. Denies hematuria. No other systemic symptoms documented.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
No significant past medical history. No prior kidney stones.

MEDICATIONS
To be initiated: Oxycodone 5 mg every 6-8 hours for pain, Tylenol for breakthrough pain

ALLERGIES
Not documented

FAMILY HISTORY
Father with history of kidney stones

SOCIAL HISTORY
Works with horses, performing manual labor including moving hay in a barn

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: Normal, afebrile, blood pressure and heart rate normal
Abdomen: No tenderness to palpation, no rebound tenderness, no guarding
CVA tenderness: Present on right side

RESULTS
CT scan: 0.5 cm stone located in proximal right ureter. No evidence of hydronephrosis.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Right-sided kidney stone, 0.5 cm in proximal right ureter without obstruction. Increase fluid intake to facilitate passage of stone. Prescribe oxycodone 5 mg every 6-8 hours for pain management with acetaminophen for breakthrough pain. Continue urine straining to capture stone. Order BMP, urinalysis, and urine culture to evaluate for infection; antibiotics may be indicated based on results. Follow-up appointment in 1-2 weeks. If stone has not passed by then, consider lithotripsy as non-invasive treatment option.
